initial_prompt: Can you explain why the sky is blue?

messages.content: Can you explain why the sky is blue?

The sky is blue because of how sunlight interacts with Earth's atmosphere—a phenomenon called Rayleigh scattering.

Sunlight contains all wavelengths of visible light. When it enters the atmosphere, it collides with gas molecules (mostly nitrogen and oxygen). These molecules are much smaller than the wavelengths of visible light, and they scatter shorter wavelengths much more strongly than longer ones—blue light scatters about 10 times more than red.

So as sunlight passes through the atmosphere, blue light gets scattered in all directions, bouncing around the sky and reaching your eyes from every angle. The other colors travel more directly through without scattering as much.

This is also why sunsets are red and orange: when the sun is near the horizon, its light travels through much more atmosphere to reach you. By then, most of the blue has scattered away, leaving the longer wavelengths—reds, oranges, yellows—to dominate.

A detail I find satisfying: the sky isn't the deepest blue possible because some violet light scatters even more than blue. But our eyes are less sensitive to violet, and some of it gets absorbed in the upper atmosphere, so we perceive the sky as blue rather than violet.
